text: Welcome to Advanced Data Science. This course adds the specializations that set senior candidates apart: boosted trees, time-series forecasting, language, and recommendations. We start with the algorithm that wins most tabular-data problems today, gradient boosting.

A random forest grows deep trees independently and averages them. Boosting does the opposite. It grows many shallow trees one after another, and each new tree is trained to fix the errors the ensemble has made so far. Start from the average, measure the residuals, fit a small tree to them, add a fraction of it, and repeat.

Here is that loop in a few lines. We start with the mean as the prediction. Each round, the residual is the actual value minus the current prediction. We fit a depth-two tree to the residuals and add a tenth of its output. That tenth is the learning rate. The word gradient comes from here: for squared error, the residual is the negative gradient of the loss.

We run this on a noisy sine wave, holding out thirty percent for testing. Test error starts at point five eight nine with just the mean, drops to point four nine three after one tree, point two five five after five, and point zero five zero after fifty. scikit-learn's GradientBoostingRegressor gives exactly the same predictions.

This is the output of the code above. After one tree, the curve is almost flat, because the step is small. After five trees, it starts to bend. After fifty, it follows the sine wave closely. Every tree removed a slice of the remaining error.

Three dials matter most. The number of trees: more trees fit tighter, and unlike a forest, too many will overfit. The learning rate: smaller steps generalize better but need more trees. And tree depth: boosting likes shallow trees, often three to six levels.
Next, we meet XGBoost, the library that made boosting fast, regularized, and famous.
